doc.title: Bobby Shew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 1, 2020

title: Fear of mistakes in music education; court trumpeters and psychology
summary: Asked about technically perfect but emotionless students, Shew traces the fear of wrong notes back through history and his own psychology classes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I had an experience like that at Boy Scout camp with a visiting troop and some song they did with rhythms that I’d never heard before. And I was wondering if you’ve ever had a student who could play technically really well but just seemed devoid of what you’re describing, that the music had no depth or emotion behind it.

Well I don’t think there’s enough paper on this planet to make a list of those people who I’ve run across in my life. It’s like the most common thing that you see, and it’s one of the kind of little personal gripes that I rabble rouse about in the field of education in the fact that it’s all become too greatly influenced, and I think from the books, some of the books that I’ve read, try to go back in history several hundred years where it became like a difficult situation for court trumpeters say for instance. If you have to do a fanfare if a visiting king and queen came in and if your chops were not in good shape and you clammed a few, like smear a couple of them on the wall, the castle wall — I read a thing in an ITG thing years and years ago where they, some research they actually decapitated a court trumpeter some times if they did a poor performance. So when you go back four, five, six hundred years you know, in Medieval times and stuff, well and who was making, there was not even a trumpet, it was they ripped a horn off of a rhinoceros or something. You know? And blew on an animal horn. And I mean and even when they started making instruments out of metal and things, it was the blacksmith when he finished with a set of horseshoes he’d make you a trumpet or a mouthpiece or something. So I mean the quality wasn’t there and I mean could you imagine I mean for a trumpet player to pick up a piece of garbage that was made by a blacksmith in between a couple of horses, you know, I mean I don’t think you’re going to work Carnegie Hall on that you know. And so the point being that this whole history of fear of making a mistake, this right and wrong issue, which — it’s something aside from music. It’s deeply embedded in the subconscious mind in the genomes of humanity of civilization, every person on the planet goes back far enough in civilization we try to survive. It’s a pro and con of

survival. The issue of right and wrong is like a gigantic social button that can get pushed and what happens is it stimulates — I mean I’m not a great psychologist but I took two years of psychology in high school ‘cause I couldn’t get into the class I wanted. It turned out to be the best mistake I ever made was to study psychology. And when I got into college I signed up for it again because I said I’ve gotta keep studying this stuff. And there’s this thing, it stimulates like the amygdala part of the brain which is the fear factor thing.
